poems:
7:00 p.m. The lasagna is still a solid.
The oven says it is done.
The oven has said that before.
Someone's fork on someone's plate, tines down.
The dog has moved to a spot that is legally not under the table.

Practice ends at seven.
Practice never ends at seven.

Rice stuck to the bottom of the pot.
Steam on the tile.
A hand pulling a hair tie off a wrist.
Seconds, noun: the food you take because the first plate went too fast to count.
Somewhere this is breakfast. Nobody here cares.
At 7:07 the dishwasher starts on its own, because somebody set the delay and will never be thanked for it.
Bread heel, nobody's.

Rinse, do not wash.
The machine needs something to do.
Knives point down.
Not the wooden spoon.
Not ever.
The van in the school lot with its engine running and both front doors open.
A kid explains a rule of a game that does not have that rule.
Onion skin near the trash, not in it.
The good scissors, found at last, cutting a pizza.
7:14, when someone announces they are not hungry and then eats standing up.
“I already told you what I wanted, and you went and did the other thing.”
Two plates in the sink and one still going, the slow eater, telling the long version.

Table wiped one direction.
Crumbs into a cupped palm.
Palm carried across the room.
Palm opened over the bin.
Half of it lands.
The salt sits closer to him than to anyone. It has been that way for years. He never arranged it.

At 7:19 the group chat lights up in three houses at once,
and dinner loses.
Chairs pushed back at four different times.
Leftovers in a container meant for something else, under a lid from a different family entirely.
The pan is soaking. The pan will soak until tomorrow. Everyone knows and no one says it.

Taped inside the cabinet:
milk
batteries
tape, the kind that works
a name and a number
ranch
Somebody at a bar is calling an appetizer dinner, and is not wrong.

Car keys.
A rolled sock.
A permission slip.
All on the same counter.
Homework starts after the plates. The plates are taking their time.
The neighbor's storm door, twice.
A table for one, phone propped against the water glass, the show already three minutes in.
The fridge opened and closed, nothing removed. Twice.
7:30. Halfway through the hour, halfway through the plate, halfway through a story about a coworker who will not be named again.

1 LG PEPPERONI
1 RANCH
DRIVER TIP 5.00
THANK YOU COME AGAIN
SURVEY CODE ON BOTTOM
Water moving behind a cabinet door.
Nobody has taken the serving spoon out. It stands in the dish like a flag on a hill nobody wanted.
The rink lobby smells the same in every state. Parents in coats, thumbs going.
A teenager at the open fridge, second dinner, eating cold rice out of the container with a serving fork.
You are being asked to try one bite. One. You have been at this negotiation before.
Kettle on, mug chosen, person elsewhere.
The oldest kid does the dishes with the resentment of an oldest kid, which is a renewable resource.
Trash bag tied, set by the door, left there long enough to become furniture.
Somebody's grandmother ate at five and finds this hour indecent.

A phone face down beside a plate.
It buzzes twice against the wood.
Then it gives up.
Ice in a glass, settling on its own.
The recipe said forty minutes. The recipe has never met this oven.
Nobody wants the last piece and nobody wants it thrown out, so it will live in foil until Thursday.
At 7:45 the practice lot empties one minivan at a time, headlights swinging across the fence.
A paper napkin, torn in half, shared.

Homework, page one.
A pencil sharpened three times
in five minutes.
The table cleared to where you could do your taxes on it, which is what it is for eleven months a year.

A screen door bangs, twice.
Whatever the month, that sound is July.
Two people talking about a third with the door mostly closed.
Sink water hot enough to hurt a little, which is the correct temperature.
7:52 and the youngest is negotiating a bath the way other people negotiate a lease.
A dish towel over a shoulder, carried into another room.
Pickup at the side door, and the smell of a gym bag arrives before the kid does.
The counter almost clean, and one jar of something with no home.
Heat still coming off the stovetop, a hand passed over it to check.
The chair he sits in has one leg that clicks. He will not fix it. It is how we know he is home.
A list of names on the fridge with checkmarks beside them, the purpose long since forgotten by everyone, including whoever made it.
The last plate goes in, the door pushed shut with a hip, and the kitchen light left on for whoever is still coming.
